Concurrently, some states focused on education. For instance, Illinois passed Public Act 103-0399, also known as "Louie's Law", which mandated that schools educate students on the dangers of fentanyl and the proper use of test strips; this law became effective on July 28, 2023. [2] <3> The Alaska Department of Health released its "2022 Drug Overdose Mortality Update" in September 2023, detailing statistics for the 2022 calendar year. [2, 4] The report, compiled by the Alaska Health Analytics and Vital Records Section and the Office of Substance Misuse and Addiction Prevention, confirmed a slight decrease in total fatal drug overdoses from 255 in 2021 to 247 in 2022. [3, 5] Despite this overall decrease, the overdose death rate for American Indian/Alaska Native (AI/AN) people remained disproportionately high and saw an increase from the previous year. [3, 5] The specific overdose death rate for the AI/AN population rose from 75.0 deaths per 100,000 in 2021 to 78.2 deaths per 100,000 in 2022. [3] In contrast, the rate for White people decreased over the same period, from 27.3 to 24.5 per 100,000. [3] The report also noted that men, individuals aged 35-44, and residents of Anchorage were other disproportionately impacted groups. [1] The funding consisted of 128 grants to clinics across 40 states and Puerto Rico to help them establish or enhance their behavioral health services. [2] The initiative is part of an ongoing effort to improve access to mental health and substance use treatment, regardless of a person's ability to pay. [1, 2] These awards are intended to help realize the vision of the Community Mental Health Act of 1963 by transforming how behavioral healthcare is delivered in communities nationwide. [1, 7] <6> Governor Roy Cooper of North Carolina officially proclaimed August 31, 2023, as 'Overdose Awareness Day' in the state. [2] The proclamation was issued to remember the lives lost to overdoses and to renew the state's commitment to ending the crisis. [2] It highlighted a severe escalation in the overdose epidemic, noting that overdose deaths had increased by 72% since 2019, a trend exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic. [2, 4] The proclamation also specified that the rates of overdose were rising fastest among Black/African American and American Indian/Indigenous communities. [2] From 2019 to 2021, the overdose death rate for Black/African American residents increased by 139%. A significant portion of this funding, $18.4 million, is allocated to broaden access to medication-assisted treatment for individuals with opioid use disorder. The study noted that the highest prevalence of xylazine-detected deaths was concentrated in the U.S. Census Bureau's Northeast region. [24] NIDA attributed this growing risk not to more common drug use, but to a more dangerous illicit drug supply, largely due to contamination from the potent synthetic opioid fentanyl in counterfeit pills resembling prescription medications. [24] <2> In a statement before the Senate Committee on Indian Affairs, the Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) Office of Justice Services (OJS) reported significant drug seizures for Fiscal Year 2023. The letter, reported on November 29, 2023, urged support for the President's supplemental funding request of $250 million for the Indian Health Service (IHS). This funding was highlighted as urgently needed to help Tribal communities address the severe impacts of the opioid and fentanyl crisis. <4> The Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) held its 26th biannual National Prescription Drug Take Back Day on October 28, 2023. [24] However, the report highlighted a counter-trend of increased danger, citing separate research that showed a dramatic rise in overdose deaths among teenagers from 2010 to 2021, a trend that continued into 2022. [24] NIDA attributed this growing risk not to more common drug use, but to a more dangerous illicit drug supply, largely due to contamination from the potent synthetic opioid fentanyl in counterfeit pills resembling prescription medications. [24] <2> In a statement before the Senate Committee on Indian Affairs, the Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) Office of Justice Services (OJS) reported significant drug seizures for Fiscal Year 2023. Operations in Indian Country led to the seizure of 1,097,671 fentanyl pills, 1,846 pounds of methamphetamine, and 98 pounds of fentanyl powder. These efforts are part of the OJS's focus on disrupting drug distribution networks that contribute to violent crime and inflict health and economic hardships on Tribal communities. The statistics cover the period from October 1, 2022, to September 30, 2023. <3> On November 6, 2023, a coalition of national tribal organizations, including the National Council of Urban Indian Health (NCUIH), the National Indian Health Board (NIHB), the National Congress of American Indians (NCAI), and the Self-Governance Communication and Education Tribal Consortium, sent a letter to U.S. Congressional leaders. The letter, reported on November 29, 2023, urged support for the President's supplemental funding request of $250 million for the Indian Health Service (IHS). This funding was highlighted as urgently needed to help Tribal communities address the severe impacts of the opioid and fentanyl crisis. <4> The Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) held its 26th biannual National Prescription Drug Take Back Day on October 28, 2023. In collaboration with law enforcement partners, the event collected 599,897 pounds of unneeded prescription medications at 4,675 collection sites across the United States. The initiative aims to prevent prescription drug misuse and addiction by providing a safe, anonymous, and no-cost method for the public to dispose of expired, unused, or unwanted medications, thereby removing them from homes where they could be mishandled or diverted. <5> On October 30, 2023, the U.S. Department of Education and the Office of National Drug Control Policy (ONDCP) issued a joint letter to educators addressing the fentanyl overdose epidemic. The letter highlighted the disproportionate impact of illicit fentanyl on young people, noting that overdose deaths among adolescents had doubled from 2019 to 2020 despite stagnant rates of youth drug use. In partnership with the Ad Council, the ONDCP's 'Real Deal on Fentanyl' campaign was promoted to educate youth on the dangers of the drug and the life-saving effects of naloxone. The letter urged schools to educate students, faculty, and parents on overdose prevention, including recognizing the signs of an overdose and administering the opioid reversal antidote naloxone, which had recently become available for over-the-counter purchase. <6> The Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) held a National Prescription Drug Take Back Day on Saturday, April 22, 2023, and the official 25th event occurred on Saturday, October 28, 2023. These events provide a safe, convenient, and anonymous way for the public to dispose of unneeded, expired, or unwanted prescription medications, including tablets, capsules, patches, and vaping devices (with lithium batteries removed), at thousands of collection sites nationwide. The initiative's goal is to prevent drug addiction and overdose deaths by removing medications that could be misused from homes. A public service announcement for the April 22, 2023 event was released on March 30, 2023. The DEA hosts this event twice a year, and beyond the specific take-back days, there are nearly 16,500 year-round disposal locations. <7> On October 19, 2023, an investigation into drug trafficking led to the arrests of Gaudencio Rosendo Perez, Zulema Cardenas Espinoza, and Alexander Samboy in connection with a major drug operation run out of the Mexzzarella Pizza parlor in the Soundview section of the Bronx. [2, 4, 6] The pizzeria is located across the street from a public school, P.S. 69. [2, 5] Authorities announced on October 23, 2023, that the seizure included over 100 pounds of cocaine, crack cocaine, fentanyl, heroin, and oxycodone, with an estimated street value of $4 million. [4] A search of the premises uncovered 42 kilograms of suspected cocaine, a kilogram of a heroin/fentanyl mixture, 1,000 envelopes of suspected oxycodone and fentanyl, a kilo press, and approximately $40,000 in cash from the basement. [3, 4] An additional 100 vials of suspected crack cocaine were found near the pizza counter. [3, 4] The operation was a collaborative effort involving federal, state, and local law enforcement agencies, including the DEA and NYPD. [4, 6] <8> The U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration's (DEA) New Jersey Division held its second annual Family Summit on Fentanyl in New Brunswick, New Jersey, on October 11, 2023. The event was one of several regional summits held by DEA field divisions in October 2023. It brought together families who have lost loved ones to drug overdoses, law enforcement, and drug prevention groups to address the fentanyl crisis. Speakers, including top state law enforcement officials like Attorney General Matt Platkin and U.S. Attorney for New Jersey Phillip Sellinger, discussed a collaborative public health approach to the crisis. The summit provided a platform for grieving families to share their experiences and transform their pain into advocacy, emphasizing that many deaths are poisonings, not overdoses. This regional event followed a national two-day summit held by the DEA in Washington D.C. on September 25-26, 2023, where Attorney General Merrick B. Garland announced $345 million in grants to combat the fentanyl epidemic.

Prediction target period: from 2025-11-23 to 2026-02-08. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> Cook County Health, in partnership with the Chicago Transit Authority (CTA), officially launched a six-month pilot program on September 15, 2025, to provide free naloxone-dispensing vending machines at five CTA rail stations. This initiative aims to combat the opioid epidemic by increasing access to the life-saving overdose-reversing medication in areas identified with higher rates of opioid-related emergencies. The five stations, chosen based on community input and emergency response data, are the 47th Street Red Line, Wilson Red/Purple Line, Jefferson Park Blue Line, Harlem/Lake Green Line, and Central Park Pink Line stations. The installations of the machines were completed in the week prior to the official launch. Cook County Health has invested $100,000 in federal American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) funds to cover the cost of the machines' installation and maintenance for the duration of the pilot. This program expands on a previous partnership between the CTA and the Chicago Department of Public Health, which saw a similar machine installed at the 95th/Dan Ryan Red Line station in late 2023. <2> The White House has proclaimed August 31 through September 6, 2025, as Overdose Prevention Week; The proclamation calls upon Americans to observe the week with programs and activities to raise awareness about the prescription opioid and drug overdose epidemic <3> On August 25, 2025, the DEA and its federal, state, and local law enforcement partners announced the disruption of a major Sinaloa Cartel-connected drug trafficking ring that distributed fentanyl, methamphetamine, cocaine, and heroin across western Washington. The organization, allegedly led by two brothers based in Sinaloa, Mexico, used semi-trucks to transport narcotics from Mexico through California into Washington, with distribution areas ranging from Whidbey Island and Arlington south to Tacoma and Lacey. The broader investigation, part of the nationwide 'Operation Take Back America' initiative, spanned 2023 and 2024. A significant series of coordinated arrests and searches occurred on August 4, 2025, which resulted in the seizure of nine kilograms of methamphetamine, over five kilograms of fentanyl, nearly four kilograms of cocaine, a kilogram of heroin, ten firearms, and over $342,000 in cash. In total, 19 individuals have been federally charged in connection with the operation. <4> New regulations for opioid prescriptions are a significant focus in 2025, implemented to address the ongoing opioid crisis by reducing the risks of misuse, addiction, and overdose. These updated guidelines introduce stricter dosage and duration limits, emphasizing the lowest effective dose for the shortest possible time; for acute pain, a duration of three days is often sufficient, with more than seven days rarely being necessary. Pain management specialists face increased documentation requirements, needing to provide detailed justifications of medical necessity, thorough patient evaluations, and risk assessments for each prescription. Furthermore, telemedicine flexibilities for prescribing opioids have been curtailed, with the DEA reinstating the requirement for an in-person evaluation before issuing long-term opioid prescriptions via telehealth, reversing temporary exceptions from the COVID-19 pandemic. <5> In observance of International Overdose Awareness Day on August 31st, the St. Cloud VA is hosting a free overdose prevention summit on Wednesday, August 27, 2025, from 10:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m. The event is open to veterans, their caregivers, and family members. The summit will provide training on how to use Narcan, identify the warning signs of an overdose, and will also provide fentanyl test strips. Registered Nurse Marcia Lindbergh explained the "C-L-L-T method" for identifying potential overdoses: 'C' for checking for deep sleep, 'L' for listening for slow or shallow breathing, the second 'L' for looking for bluish or grayish skin, and 'T' for touching for clammy skin. In addition to the St. Cloud event, similar events will be held at the Alexandria V.A. clinic on August 26th and the Brainerd V.A. clinic on August 28th. <6> A narrative review titled 'Postmarketing Research for Opioid Abuse-Deterrent Formulations: A Narrative Review' was accepted for publication in the Journal of Pain Research, an international, open-access journal. [1, 2] The review, authored by Lynn Webster and colleagues, summarizes postmarketing studies to evaluate the effectiveness of abuse-deterrent formulations (ADFs) of opioids currently available in the US. [1] It notes that while the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) requires post-approval evaluation for ADFs, none of the four currently designated opioid ADFs have attained the additional category 4 labeling based on postmarket studies. [1] The review identified relevant studies through PubMed searches and cited literature, including data from sources like the Researched Abuse, Diversion, and Addiction-Related Surveillance (RADARS) System. [1, 6] The findings suggest that ADFs, particularly XTAMPZA ER, have been associated with reduced non-oral abuse or misuse compared to non-ADF formulations. [1] However, some research indicates that the long-term benefits in reducing harm are not clearly established. [7] <7> A report on Dutchess County's emergency medical services (EMS) for the second quarter of 2025 (April-June) revealed that rural communities continue to face the longest response times, despite a supplemental ambulance service launched by the county six months prior. [2] The data, published in August 2025, shows that the volunteer-based ambulance services in towns like Pine Plains and Milan are still not meeting national benchmarks. [2] For Priority 1 calls, which include life-threatening emergencies like drug overdoses, Pine Plains recorded an average response time of 12 minutes and 58 seconds. [2] While this was an improvement from the first quarter's 13:56, it remains significantly above the 9-minute national standard. [2] In Milan, the average response time for Priority 1 calls worsened, increasing from 12:48 in the first quarter to 15:05 in the second. [2] Countywide, there was a slight improvement, with 71% of all Priority 1 calls being reached within nine minutes, up from 67% in the first quarter. [2] County Executive Sue Serino stated that residents across the county are benefiting from the supplemental coverage, which ensures an ambulance responds to all medical calls, and that the program will continue to improve. [2] <8> In September 2023, the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) launched an investigation into methamphetamine traffickers in the Billings, Montana area. As part of the investigation, from September to October 2023, the DEA utilized confidential sources to buy just under one and a half pounds of pure methamphetamine from Julia Renee Arvizo, 47. Investigators also learned that Arvizo had traded methamphetamine for firearms and had told a confidential source in November 2023 that she could supply three pounds of the drug at one time. Arvizo pleaded guilty to possession with intent to distribute methamphetamine in January 2025 and was subsequently sentenced to 10 years in prison, to be followed by five years of supervised release. The case was part of Project Safe Neighborhoods, a national initiative aimed at reducing violent crime. <9> A Hobbs, New Mexico woman, Amber Dawn Rogers Johnson, 39, was sentenced to 19 years in federal prison following a high-speed chase that exposed a major drug trafficking operation. [3] On April 7, 2025, Johnson pleaded guilty to two counts of possession with intent to distribute methamphetamine, two counts of possession with intent to distribute fentanyl, and one count of using and carrying a firearm during and in relation to a drug trafficking crime. [3] The investigation and bust on November 9, 2023, resulted in the total seizure of approximately 1.7 kilograms of fentanyl, 827 grams of methamphetamine, and five firearms. [3] The events leading to her arrest included a chase that crossed into Texas, during which Johnson shot at deputies and discarded a backpack containing drugs and firearms. [3] Upon her release, she will be under five years of supervised supervision. [3] <10> On May 2, 2025, federal agents arrested Alex Anthony Martinez at his Albuquerque, New Mexico residence as part of a coordinated, multi-state operation targeting a fentanyl trafficking organization. This operation was notable for resulting in the largest single seizure of fentanyl pills in the history of the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA). The initial announcement of the multi-state bust, which involved 16 arrests across five states, came around May 6-7, 2025. Martinez, identified as a "regional manager" for the trafficking network, was later convicted by a federal jury, with the verdict being announced on August 7, 2025.
